Case report 
A case of childhood stiﬀ-person syndrome with striatal lesions: A
possible entity distinct from the classical adult form 
Masafumi Sanefuji a,⇑, Hiroyuki Torisu a, Ryutaro Kira a,
Hiroshi Yamashita b, Kazuna Ejima a, Hiroshi Shigeto c, Yui Takada a,
Keiko Yoshida b, Toshiro Hara a
a Department of Pediatri cs, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kyushu University, Japan 
b Departme nt of Neurops ychiatry, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kyushu Universit y, Japan 
c Departme nt of Neurolo gy, Neurologica l Institute, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kyushu Universit y, Japan 
Received 18 March 2012; received in revised form 30 July 2012; accepted 5 August 2012 
Abstract
Parainfectious or autoimmune striatal lesions have been repeatedly described in children. We report a 7-year-old girl with painful 
muscle spasms, leading to the diagnosis of childhood stiﬀ-person syndrome (SPS). Striatal lesions were demonstrated by diﬀusion-
weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and single-photon emission computed tomography but not by conventional MRI.
Autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) were absent. Steroid pulse therapy and high-dose intravenous immu- 
noglobulin resolved all the symptoms with slight sequelae. Childhood SPS may be characterized by absent anti-GAD antibodies 
and a transient benign clinical course, and it may have a pathomechanism distinct from that in adult SPS.

Patient s show a wide range of neuropsychi atric symp-

depression, and obsessive–compuls ive behavior s.
We report a girl exhibiting obsessi ve–compulsive 
behaviors, muscle rigid ity, and letha rgy, as well as pain-

3. Dis cussion 
The present case exh ibited episodi c, painful spasms 
and obsessi ve–compulsive behavior s, follo wed by
letha rgy and muscl e rigi dity. DWI of MRI and SPECT 
disclo sed bilateral stri atal lesi ons. The presence of ante- 
ceden t infec tion and good respo nse to immuno modula- 
tory therapy suggest s an autoimmun e pathogenes is.
Lethargy , rigid ity, and obsessive–compulsive behaviors 
have been report ed with striatal lesio ns [3]. The follow- 
ing frontal lobe sympt oms with front al hyp oactivit y in
SPEC T could be accoun ted for in the context of the 
cortic o-striatal- thalamo-cor tica l circui t. But episodic 
spasm s have been scarce ly associ ated with striata l
lesion s.
SPS is an uncommon autoimmune disorde r of the 
centra l nervou s syst em, charact erized by progres sive 
rigidit y and episodic painful spasm s. Classi cal SPS in
adulthood is characteriz ed by a chronic, slowly progres -
sive clini cal course over months or years, frequent ly with 
anti-GAD antibodies and psychia tric symptoms such as
anxiety disorde rs [4]. On the oth er hand, children 
repo rted with SPS exhibit acute onset and a trans ient 
benign course with no or slight sequela e and usuall y
do not have anti-GAD antibodi es [5–8], as with our 
patient. To our know ledge, psyc hiatric sympto ms have
never been reported , althoug h they cou ld be overlooked.
Chi ldhood SPS may repres ent an entity distinct from 
adulthood SPS.

The pathophysi ologic al mechan ism of childhood SPS 
is unclear . In adulthood SPS, the pathology has dis- 
closed spinal and brain stem lesi ons but no cortical 
lesi ons [9]. Brain and spinal MRI detect no abno rmali- 
ties in most cases, althoug h T2-weight ed MRI have
reveal ed a variety of lesio ns in the tempor al lobes, hypo- 
thala mus, pons, spinal cord, hippocampu s, and striatum

pathology has never been report ed. MRI reveal ed no
abnormalities except the hipp ocampal lesi on in one 
child [5–8]. To the best of our knowl edge, there are no
DWI and SPECT data in adults and childr en with 
SPS. Dysfuncti on of the stria tum resul ts in a variety of
movem ent disorde rs. The striatum lesions demonst rated 
by DWI and SPECT may account for the episodi c
spasm s in our patie nt. The origin of childhood SPS 
might be the striatum , which is more commonl y
involv ed in childhood than in adulthood.
In conclusi on, the present case suggest s that child- 
hood SPS may have a pathome chanism distinct from 
that in adu lt SPS, but furt her report s with DWI and 
SPEC T are need ed to conﬁrm this hypo thesis.
